candidates.statement: Then the linear transformation described by the matrix $T$ can be seen in the following way, which we shall generalize later on:
A categorified version of this process should be a 2-functor.

Since we want to think of $X$ as a category, rather than look at functions from the objects of $X$ into $\mathbb{C}$, we should look at functors from $X$ into some category which plays the role of $\mathbb{C}$.
A similar caveat should apply in the categorified setting.
Note that, in particular, essentially finitely generated groupoids must be essentially finite, since every object has an identity morphism.

The idea is that given a span of groupoids, as in Figure [2](#fig:grpd-span){reference-type="ref" reference="fig:grpd-span"} (which suppresses the homomorphisms labelling the strands in the span, but should be compared with Figure [1](#fig:set-span){reference-type="ref" reference="fig:set-span"}), there will be a "transfer" 2-linear map from the KV 2-vector space associated to the source of the span, to that associated to the target.

Since groupoids naturally form a 2-category, we should weaken the notion of composition, and give an appropriate notion of 2-morphism, for a bicategory $\operatorname{Span}(\boldsymbol{\operatorname{{FinGpd}}})$.

For the most part, since the construction we mean to give is invariant under equivalence of groupoids, and taking the $A_i$ to be skeletal makes this strict, we will assume strict commutativity, though we shall indicate where the argument must be changed to accommodate the weak case.
When we apply $\Lambda$, these duals will in fact become adjoints, as we shall see.

Since it makes sense to speak of two objects of a groupoid being isomorphic, the weakest meaningful condition is that objects of groupoids $X$ and $X'$ should need only project to isomorphic objects on $A_2$.
Since the categorified setting has more layers of structure, there is a choice of level to which the structure in the concept of a vector space should be lifted.
Thus it should not be surprising that KV 2-vector spaces have a structure analogous to free vector spaces generated by some finite set - which are isomorphic to $\mathbb{C}^k$.
The standard example of this approach is the Kapranov-Voevodsky (KV) definition of a 2-vector space [@KV], which is the form we shall use (at least when the situation is finite-dimensional).
To motivate the KV definition, consider the idea that, in categorifying, one should replace the base field $\mathbb{C}$ with a monoidal category.
But we should define these precisely.

$E$ should be an additive functor with $E(X_i) = V_i$, where $V_i$ is the $k$-tuple of vector spaces having the zero vector space in every position except the $i^{th}$, which has a copy of $\mathbb{C}$.

A natural transformation $\alpha$ between these should assign, to every object $X \in \boldsymbol{\operatorname{{Vect}}}^n$, a morphism $\alpha_X : T(X) \mathop{\rightarrow}T'(X)$ in $\boldsymbol{\operatorname{{Vect}}}^m$, such that the usual naturality square commutes for every morphism $f : X \mathop{\rightarrow}Y$ in $\boldsymbol{\operatorname{{Vect}}}^n$.

Then a morphism $\alpha_X : T(X) \mathop{\rightarrow}T'(X)$ consists of an $m$-tuple of linear maps: $$\alpha_j : \oplus_{k=1}^{n} V_{j,k} \otimes X_k \mathop{\rightarrow}\oplus_{k=1}^{n} V'_{j,k} \otimes X_k$$ but by the universal property of the biproduct, this is the same as having an $(n \times m)$-indexed set of maps $$\alpha_{jk} : V_{j,k} \otimes X_k \mathop{\rightarrow}\oplus_{r=1}^{n} V'_{j,r} \otimes X_r$$ and by the dual universal property, this is the same as having $(n \times n \times m)$-indexed maps $$\alpha_{jkr} : V_{j,k} \otimes X_k \mathop{\rightarrow}V'_{j,r} \otimes X_r$$ However, we must have the naturality condition for every morphism $f:X \mathop{\rightarrow}X'$: $$\xymatrix{ T(X) \ar[d]_{\alpha_{X}} \ar[r]^{T(f)} & T(X') \ar[d]^{\alpha_{X'}} \\ T'(X) \ar[r]_{T'(f)} & T'(X')\\ }$$ Note that each of the arrows in this diagram is a morphism in $\boldsymbol{\operatorname{{Vect}}}^m$, which are linear maps in each component---so in fact we have a separate naturality square for each component.
A relevant class of examples, as we shall show, come from special kinds of groupoids.
(We also should note that, since our groupoids are discrete, there is no distinction here between sheaves and presheaves).
candidates.section_title: Free 2-Vector Space on a Finite Groupoid

candidates.statement: If $F : \boldsymbol{\operatorname{{X}}}\mathop{\rightarrow}\boldsymbol{\operatorname{{Vect}}}$ is as above, there should be a canonical isomorphism between $[G,f^{\ast}(F)]$ (a hom-set in $[\boldsymbol{\operatorname{{Y}}},\boldsymbol{\operatorname{{Vect}}}]$) and $[p_{\ast}(G),F]$ (a hom-set in $[\boldsymbol{\operatorname{{X}}},\boldsymbol{\operatorname{{Vect}}}]$).
We shall want to make use of the units and counits from both the adjunction in which $f_{\ast}$ is a left adjoint, and that in which it is a right adjoint.
Once again, it is useful for practical calculations to have a coordinate-dependent form for these maps, but there is a convenient intrinsic definition which we shall describe first.

To begin with, we should describe the functors $f^{\ast} f_{\ast}$ ("push-pull"), which is an endofunctor on $[\boldsymbol{\operatorname{{Y}}},\boldsymbol{\operatorname{{Vect}}}]$, and $f_{\ast} f^{\ast}$ ("pull-push"), which is an endofunctor on $[\boldsymbol{\operatorname{{X}}},\boldsymbol{\operatorname{{Vect}}}]$.

Since the adjunction is ambidextrous, it applies in both cases, but to describe the unit and counit properly, we should note that in general the canonical description of the left and right adjunctions are different.
In particular, we first must describe how our 2-functor $\Lambda$ will produce 2-linear maps from spans of groupoids.
That is, the composition of the 2-linear maps must be compatible, in a weak sense, with composition of spans of groupoids.
For each $x'$, this must be an isomorphism between the above vector spaces.

Given $m_1 \otimes v_1$ and $m_2 \otimes v_2$ representing the same element $m \otimes v$ of $\mathbb{C}[Aut(t(x)] \otimes_{\mathbb{C}[Aut({x})]} F(x)$, we must have $h_1 \in Aut(x)$ with $$m_1 t(h_1) = m_2$$ and $$h_1 v_2 = v_1$$ But then applying $\gamma^{-1}$, we get: $$\gamma^{-1}(m_1 \otimes v_1) = (1 \otimes v_1)_{m_1^{-1}} = (1 \otimes h_1 v_2)_{m_1^{-1}}$$ and $$\gamma^{-1}(m_2 \otimes v_2) = (1 \otimes v_2)_{m_2^{-1}} = (1 \otimes v_2)_{t(h_1)^{-1} m_1^{-1}}$$ but these are in the same component, since $g \sim g'$ when $g' s'(k) = t(h) g$ for some $h \in Aut(x)$ and $k \in Aut({x'})$.
For our construction to give a 2-functor, this must agree with composition in two ways.
We also must show that $\Lambda$ respects horizontal composition weakly.

By commutativity for the span of span maps (which is necessarily strict here!), we also must have that $$\bigoplus_{[y'] | t(y') \cong t(y)} \mathbb{C}[Aut(t(y))] \otimes_{\mathbb{C}[Aut(y')]}G(y') \cong \bigoplus_{[y'] | s(y') \cong s(y)} \mathbb{C}[Aut(s(y))] \otimes_{\mathbb{C}[Aut(y)]}\mathbb{C}$$

::: proof *Proof.* The argument here is similar to that in Theorem [\[thm:groupoidification\]](#thm:groupoidification){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:groupoidification"}, except that we must deal with nontrivial representations of the $Aut(x_i)$.

The coherence conditions for the compositor morphisms $$\beta_{S,T} : \Lambda(T \circ S) \mathop{\rightarrow}\Lambda(T) \circ \Lambda(S)$$ and the associator say that these must make the following diagram commute for all composable triples $(X,X',X'')$: $$\label{eq:wk2fncassoc} \xy (0,20)*+{\Lambda(X'') \circ \Lambda(X') \circ \Lambda(X)}="top"; (35,4)*+{\Lambda(X'' \circ X') \circ \Lambda(X)}="rttop"; (25,-20)*+{\Lambda( (X'' \circ X') \circ X )}="rtbot"; (-25,-20)*+{\Lambda(X'' \circ (X' \circ X) )}="leftbot"; (-35,4)*+{\Lambda(X'') \circ \Lambda(X' \circ X)}="leftop"; {\ar^{1 \otimes \beta_{2,1}} "leftop";"top"} {\ar_{\beta_{3,2} \otimes 1} "rttop";"top"} {\ar^{\beta_{3,21}} "leftbot";"leftop"} {\ar_{\beta_{32,1}} "rtbot";"rttop"} {\ar_{\Lambda(\alpha_{X'',X',X})} "leftbot";"rtbot"} \endxy$$

In general, the coherence conditions for the "unit" isomorphism $$U_A : 1_{\Lambda(A)} \stackrel{\sim}{\mathop{\rightarrow}} \Lambda(1_A)$$ which accomplishes weak preservation of identities, say that it must make the following commute for any span $X: A_1 \mathop{\rightarrow}A_2$: $$\label{eq:wk2fncunit} \xymatrix{ \Lambda(X) & & \\ & & \\ \Lambda(X) \circ \Lambda(1_{A_1}) \ar[uu]_{1 \otimes U_{A_1}} & & \Lambda(X \circ 1_{A_1})\ar[uull]_{\Lambda(r_X)} \ar[ll]_{\beta_{X,1_{A_1}}} }$$ where $r_{A_1}$ is the right unitor for $A_1$.
